crossAddiction.name: Swapping one addiction for another
crossAddiction.oneLiner: Getting free of one addiction makes a new one less likely, not more: within three years, 13.1% of people who recovered picked up a new one, against 27.2% of those who did not.

axes.classification: Not a diagnosis. DSM-5 and ICD-11 diagnose each substance or behaviour separately; 'cross-addiction', 'addiction transfer' and 'addiction substitution' are informal or research terms.

crossAddiction.axesNote: Boundary page about moving between addictions, so the per-addiction axes do not apply; the nulls are deliberate. Withdrawal and overdose safety come from the page of each substance involved.

safety.text: After gastric bypass, alcohol peaks faster and higher in the blood, and new drinking problems start to rise from the second year after surgery. If you have had weight-loss surgery, treat any rise in drinking as a warning sign and tell your care team.

timeline.label: After gastric bypass: new alcohol problems rise from year 2
timeline.note: Hours since surgery, not since last use. Alcohol-problem symptoms: 7.6% the year before surgery, 7.3% at year 1, 9.6% at year 2. By year 5, 20.8% had new symptoms after bypass vs 11.3% after banding. No peak seen; follow-up ended at 7 years.

markers.label: Year 2 after gastric bypass: first measurable rise in alcohol problems

beliefs.voice: If I quit this, I'll just replace it with something else.
beliefs.science: Of 34,653 US adults, those who recovered from one substance problem picked up a new one half as often as those who did not (13.1% vs 27.2%). Studies find recovery spreading three times as often as swapping.
beliefs.beliefSource: Blanco 2014 describes it as what remitters 'are often thought' to face and calls it 'clinical lore'; Kim 2021's title asks 'Clinical lore or empirically-based?'. First person: 'Just feels like I traded one drug for another' (recovery-testimonials/02-reddit-leaves-cannabis.md, B3).

beliefs.voice: I can only quit one thing at a time.
beliefs.science: In 35 trials, adding stop-smoking help during alcohol or drug recovery raised quit rates and left other abstinence unchanged (RR 0.97). One 499-person trial found drinking outcomes worse when smoking treatment started during intensive alcohol treatment.
beliefs.beliefSource: Documented as a clinicians' worry: 'Fear of jeopardizing drinking outcomes' (Joseph 2004); concern that 'recovery from other addictions could be compromised' (Apollonio 2016). No survey of the public's version was found.

beliefs.voice: If I stop smoking, I'll drink more.
beliefs.science: In three US quit studies (1,022 smokers), drinkers' drinking fell and stayed lower at 26 weeks. A 2004 meta-analysis linked smoking help during addiction treatment with a 25% higher chance of long-term sobriety.
beliefs.beliefSource: Clinicians' concern documented in Joseph 2004 and Apollonio 2016 (see belief above); the public's version was not surveyed in this pass.

beliefs.voice: It's a different thing, so it doesn't count.
beliefs.science: Among people recovered from drug problems, those who kept smoking had twice the odds of relapse (OR 2.02). Recovered drinkers who smoked daily had 54% higher odds of alcohol dependence returning. When swaps happen, outcomes tend to be poorer.
beliefs.beliefSource: First person: 'Quit drinking alcohol 9 years ago and replaced it with weed' (recovery-testimonials/02-reddit-leaves-cannabis.md, line 94); that file notes substitution 'runs both ways and nobody seems to see it coming'.

whatWorks.what: Get stop-smoking medication during alcohol or drug recovery rather than putting it off
whatWorks.note: Cochrane 2016, 35 trials: medication raised tobacco abstinence (RR 1.60), counselling plus medication RR 1.74, alcohol and drug abstinence unchanged. Graded low quality; one trial favoured waiting until intensive alcohol treatment ends.

whatWorks.what: Watch for a new habit taking over the coping job
whatWorks.note: In 185 people recovered from gambling, the usual reason for a swap was coping. Swappers had more childhood adversity, impulsivity and trouble handling emotions. Across studies: male, younger, more severe, mental-health problems.

whatWorks.what: When you deal with one addiction, check for the others
whatWorks.note: Gambling problems overlap heavily with nicotine, alcohol and drug problems in national surveys; the authors recommend screening for the other conditions when treatment starts.

whatWorks.what: Before and after weight-loss surgery: alcohol education and regular screening
whatWorks.note: Recommended by the authors of the 7-year LABS-2 follow-up, which found one in five bypass patients reported new alcohol-problem symptoms within 5 years.

numbers.stat: US adults with a substance use disorder, 2001-02 to 2004-05: 13.1% of those who recovered developed a new one within about 3 years, vs 27.2% of those who did not recover.
73.2% of US adults with lifetime pathological gambling (2001-02 survey) also had an alcohol use disorder; 60.4% had nicotine dependence.
20.8% of gastric bypass patients reported new alcohol-problem symptoms within 5 years of surgery (US, LABS-2, surgery 2006-09).

placeholders.wanted: When, after quitting a substance or behaviour, the risk of a new addiction shows up (weeks, months, years).
placeholders.why: Blanco 2014 measured one 3-year window and no study found here times substitution after quitting; only weight-loss surgery has a measured time course.

placeholders.wanted: A validated screener for addiction substitution.
placeholders.why: None found. The page should send readers to the screener on each addiction's own page.

placeholders.wanted: Behaviour-to-behaviour swaps (porn to gaming, betting to crypto trading) and their rates.
placeholders.why: Kim 2021 found gambling was the starting addiction in only 2.08% of 96 studies; behaviour-to-behaviour swapping is almost unstudied.

placeholders.wanted: Evidence that ordinary readers (not clinicians) hold 'one thing at a time' and 'quitting smoking will make me drink'.
placeholders.why: Sources document the clinicians' version only; no survey of the public's beliefs was found in this pass.

placeholders.wanted: Cannabis used as a substitute for alcohol or opioids: does it help or hurt recovery?
placeholders.why: Not researched in this pass; opioids and cannabis are the most-studied starting addictions in Kim 2021, so the evidence exists to be read.

frameworkFindings.topic: Most people recover, many without formal treatment
frameworkFindings.finding: US lifetime remission: 83.7% nicotine, 90.6% alcohol, 97.2% cannabis, 99.2% cocaine; half remitted about 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after onset. 77.5% of recovered drinkers had no help or treatment; in a 2017 survey 53.9% used some help, mostly mutual-help groups.
frameworkFindings.implication: Open each page with the base rate: most people get out. Give the median years honestly, since they are long. Do not imply treatment is the only route, nor that help is pointless.

frameworkFindings.finding: US adults who resolved an alcohol or drug problem made a median of 2 serious attempts (mean 5.35, skewed); it did not differ by substance. Smoking estimates run from 6.1 to 142 attempts depending on method; the authors' least-biased figure is 29.6.
frameworkFindings.implication: Say 'most people need more than one go' and quote the median, as the authors advise. For smoking, say the number is uncertain. Frame a failed attempt as the normal route, never as a score.

frameworkFindings.topic: Relapse risk is front-loaded, then eases
frameworkFindings.finding: Hunt 1971 found nicotine, heroin and alcohol relapse curves almost identical over a year: most relapse early, then the rate slows sharply. A review of 20 alcohol and tobacco studies found the same shape. Relapse rates resemble those in hypertension, asthma and type 2 diabetes.
frameworkFindings.implication: The timeline can honestly show risk highest early and easing with time. Pair it with 'relapse is common, as in other long-term illnesses' so a slip reads as expected, not as proof of failure.

frameworkFindings.topic: Cue-craving can grow before it fades (incubation)
frameworkFindings.finding: Paid-abstinent smokers showed more cue-craving at day 35 than day 7; alcohol inpatients peaked at day 60; in cocaine users a brain marker peaked at 1-6 months while self-rated craving fell. Twenty clinical opioid studies found no rise.
frameworkFindings.implication: Never draw cue-craving falling to zero. Show background craving fading while cue-reactivity may hold or rise for weeks to months, labelled 'found for some substances'. Do not apply it to opioids.

frameworkFindings.topic: Craving follows cues and access, not the clock
frameworkFindings.finding: Flight attendants' craving peaked as landing neared, on short and long flights alike. Orthodox Jewish smokers craved less on the Sabbath than on a forced-abstinence workday. People who expect a chance to use report stronger urges. Smokers' first lapses came where cigarettes were available.
frameworkFindings.implication: Draw craving as spikes tied to situations, not a smooth decay by hour. Tell readers that removing access lowers craving itself, which backs the 'remove the supply' advice from the testimonial synthesis.

frameworkFindings.topic: Expecting bad withdrawal predicts worse withdrawal (nocebo)
frameworkFindings.finding: Expected distress predicted opiate withdrawal severity; dose did not. Smokers expecting strong withdrawal reported worse symptoms. 17% of patients stopping a placebo reported discontinuation symptoms. Explicit symptom suggestions and watching others suffer are among the strongest nocebo triggers.
frameworkFindings.implication: A vivid symptom list can add symptoms. Lead with what most people do not get, show ranges rather than dramatic peaks, keep horror stories off the page, and keep only danger signs vivid.

frameworkFindings.topic: Preparing people helps when it is framed well
frameworkFindings.finding: Across 105 surgery trials, psychological preparation, including what sensations to expect, gave low-quality evidence of less pain and negative affect. Five of six framing studies found positive framing ('70% will not get it') reduced nocebo effects. A 1994 trial reportedly cut withdrawal complaints by telling smokers to expect none (unverified).
frameworkFindings.implication: Do not hide the timeline; frame it. For each phase: what is normal, how many people do not get it, when it eases, what to do. Information framed this way beats silence.

frameworkFindings.finding: In 893 smokers, every withdrawal feature (severity, slope, curvature, day-to-day volatility) varied widely between people. Rising or volatile symptoms predicted relapse. Medication lowered severity but did not change the shape over time.
frameworkFindings.implication: Draw each track as a band with a typical line inside, never a single curve. Add 'yours may differ'. Flag symptoms that rise instead of easing as a reason to get support.

frameworkFindings.finding: 'Dependence' means two things: uncontrolled use, and the body adapting to a drug. DSM-5 does not count opioid tolerance or withdrawal when opioids are taken solely under appropriate medical supervision. Severity: mild 2-3 criteria, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more.
frameworkFindings.implication: Pages with a prescribed origin (opioids, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, gabapentinoids) say plainly that withdrawal alone does not mean addiction. Keep 'body adapted' and 'cannot control it' apart everywhere.

frameworkFindings.topic: After a break, the old dose can kill
frameworkFindings.finding: Across six prison systems, drug-related death was 3 to 8 times higher in the first 2 weeks after release than in weeks 3-12, and still raised in weeks 3-4. After inpatient opiate detox, all three overdose deaths within four months were among those who completed it.
frameworkFindings.implication: Pages with overdoseRiskAfterBreak true put a danger marker at the return to use, not at quitting: 'your tolerance is gone; the old amount can kill'. Place it inside the good stretch.

frameworkFindings.topic: Brain recovery: real, partial, and over-sold
frameworkFindings.finding: Volkow 2001 scanned 5 methamphetamine users: dopamine transporters rose 16-19% after 12-17 months abstinent, but test scores did not improve significantly. A 2022 review of 45 studies found mostly partial recovery. The brain-disease model is disputed. 'Dopamine fasting' does not lower dopamine.
frameworkFindings.implication: Say 'the brain partly recovers over months' and cite the review, not one coloured scan. No 'reset your dopamine' claims, no day-counts for brain healing, no brain images offered as proof.

frameworkFindings.topic: Rock bottom and 'you have to want it'
frameworkFindings.finding: Court-mandated patients did as well as or better than others at 1 and 5 years. Compulsory detention showed no clear benefit and possible harm. Family training (CRAFT) got about two-thirds of treatment-refusing people into treatment. 'Hitting bottom' had no formal definition until 2017.
frameworkFindings.implication: Every page rejects 'wait for rock bottom'. Pressure from a court, partner or job can start recovery that works. Add one line for family members pointing to CRAFT; never endorse locked detention.

frameworkFindings.topic: The good stretch and the bad moment
frameworkFindings.finding: In young heavy drinkers, good-mood days raised urges, which raised intoxication. But smokers' first lapses came with bad mood, cues and easy access, and positive mood did not predict smoking relapse in 450 smokers. Evidence for the good-stretch hazard is mostly from first-person accounts.
frameworkFindings.implication: Warn about both the bad night and the good stretch. Present the good-stretch risk as a pattern people report, with the trial evidence labelled 'young drinkers', not as proven for every addiction.

frameworkFindings.topic: What happens after the first slip
frameworkFindings.finding: Marlatt's abstinence-violation effect says a slip plus self-blame spirals into relapse. Real-time data only partly agree: those measures mostly failed to predict progression, but smokers who felt like giving up after a first lapse lapsed again faster; trying to recover the same day slowed it.
frameworkFindings.implication: Each page gets an 'if you slipped' line: one use is not the end; get back on track that day. Avoid visuals that reset to zero, since they invite the 'I've blown it' reaction.

frameworkFindings.topic: Showing uncertainty costs little trust; tables teach, graphics attract
frameworkFindings.finding: In five experiments (n=5,780), stating uncertainty only slightly lowered trust, mostly when phrased in words rather than numbers. A drug facts table raised correct grasp of a statin's benefit from 9% to 72%. An infographic was liked more than plain text but taught no more.
frameworkFindings.implication: Show ranges as numbers ('24-72 hours'), not 'roughly'. Show an evidence grade on each block. Treat the timeline graphic as the hook and the short table or text beneath it as what teaches.

frameworkFindings.finding: 516 clinicians who read about 'a substance abuser' judged the person more to blame and deserving punishment than with 'has a substance use disorder'. In 1,288 adults, 'addict', 'alcoholic' and 'substance abuser' carried strong negative bias; 'recurrence of use' scored better than 'relapse'.
frameworkFindings.implication: Use 'addiction' for the topic, since readers search it, but never label the reader: 'people who drink heavily', not 'alcoholics'. Prefer 'slip' or 'return to use' over 'relapse' in reader-facing lines.

refs.cite: Kelly JF, Finney JW, Moos R (2005). Substance use disorder patients who are mandated to treatment: characteristics, treatment process, and 1- and 5-year outcomes. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 28:213-223.
refs.supports: n=2,095: mandated patients had similar or better 1- and 5-year outcomes, similar treatment gains.

refs.cite: Werb D, Kamarulzaman A, Meacham MC, et al. (2016). The effectiveness of compulsory drug treatment: a systematic review. International Journal of Drug Policy 28:1-9.
refs.supports: Nine studies: compulsory treatment not shown to improve outcomes; some suggest harms.

refs.cite: Klag S, O'Callaghan F, Creed P (2005). The use of legal coercion in the treatment of substance abusers: an overview and critical analysis of thirty years of research. Substance Use & Misuse 40:1777-1795.
refs.supports: Thirty years of coercion research: mixed, inconsistent, inconclusive results.

refs.cite: Roozen HG, de Waart R, van der Kroft P (2010). Community reinforcement and family training: an effective option to engage treatment-resistant substance-abusing individuals in treatment. Addiction 105:1729-1738.
refs.supports: CRAFT engaged about two-thirds of treatment-resistant patients; 3x Al-Anon, 2x Johnson intervention.

refs.cite: Kirouac M, Witkiewitz K (2017). Identifying 'hitting bottom' among individuals with alcohol problems: development and evaluation of the NADIR. Substance Use & Misuse 52:1602-1615.
refs.supports: 'Hitting bottom' widely portrayed as necessary but had never been formally operationalized.

refs.cite: Bold KW, Fucito LM, Corbin WR, et al. (2016). Daily relations among affect, urge, targeted naltrexone, and alcohol use in young adults. Experimental and Clinical Psychopharmacology 24:367-375.
refs.supports: 127 young heavy drinkers: positive affect raised urge, which raised odds of intoxication.

refs.cite: Roos CR, Bold KW, Witkiewitz K, et al. (2021). Reward drinking and naltrexone treatment response among young adult heavy drinkers. Addiction 116:2360-2371.
refs.supports: 62.2% were 'reward drinkers'; naltrexone weakened the same-day positive affect-urge link.

refs.cite: Heffner JL, Mull KE, McClure JB, Bricker JB (2018). Positive affect as a predictor of smoking cessation and relapse. Substance Use & Misuse 53:980-988.
refs.supports: 450 smokers: no depressive-symptom domain, including positive affect, predicted relapse.

refs.cite: Curry S, Marlatt GA, Gordon JR (1987). Abstinence violation effect: validation of an attributional construct with smoking cessation. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 55:145-149.
refs.supports: Original AVE validation; no abstract retrieved, so findings unverified here.

refs.cite: Shiffman S, Hickcox M, Paty JA, et al. (1996). Progression from a smoking lapse to relapse: prediction from abstinence violation effects, nicotine dependence, and lapse characteristics. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 64:993-1002.
refs.supports: AVE indicators mostly failed; 'felt like giving up' sped second lapse; restorative coping slowed it.

refs.cite: Kirchner TR, Shiffman S, Wileyto EP (2012). Relapse dynamics during smoking cessation: recurrent abstinence violation effects and lapse-relapse progression. Journal of Abnormal Psychology 121:187-197.
refs.supports: First-lapse AVE responses did not predict relapse; later drops in self-efficacy sped progression.

refs.cite: van der Bles AM, van der Linden S, Freeman ALJ, Spiegelhalter DJ (2020). The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers. PNAS 117:7672-7683.
refs.supports: Five experiments, n=5,780: uncertainty only slightly reduced trust, mostly for verbal wording.

refs.cite: Schwartz LM, Woloshin S, Welch HG (2009). Using a drug facts box to communicate drug benefits and harms: two randomized trials. Annals of Internal Medicine 150:516-527.
refs.supports: Facts box: 72% vs 9% correctly quantified statin benefit.

refs.cite: Buljan I, Malički M, Wager E, et al. (2018). No difference in knowledge obtained from infographic or plain language summary of a Cochrane systematic review: three randomized controlled trials. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 97:86-94.
refs.supports: Infographic preferred for reading experience but gave no more knowledge than plain-language text.

refs.cite: Spiegelhalter D, Pearson M, Short I (2011). Visualizing uncertainty about the future. Science 333:1393-1400.
refs.supports: Limited experimental evidence on how uncertainty visualisations are understood; depends on numeracy.

refs.cite: Kelly JF, Westerhoff CM (2010). Does it matter how we refer to individuals with substance-related conditions? A randomized study of two commonly used terms. International Journal of Drug Policy 21:202-207.
refs.supports: 516 clinicians: 'substance abuser' raised culpability and punishment judgments vs 'substance use disorder'.

refs.cite: Ashford RD, Brown AM, Curtis B (2018). Substance use, recovery, and linguistics: the impact of word choice on explicit and implicit bias. Drug and Alcohol Dependence 189:131-138.
refs.supports: 1,288 adults: 'addict', 'alcoholic', 'substance abuser' strongly negative; 'recurrence of use' beat 'relapse'.
